subject: PrivGPU admission and slab elasticity: network slicing & failover choreography

Subject: PrivGPU admission and slab elasticity: network slicing & failover choreography

Hi Sanjay / EdgeCarve infra team —

Thanks for the capacity numbers you sent yesterday. Before our architecture review on Thursday I wanted to surface a proposed admission and slab-elasticity plan so we can confirm operational commitments and the fallback story. High-level ask: please review the attached capacity model (capacity-model-v3.xlsx) and the network-slice diagram (warm-pool-slice-diagram.pdf) and call out any hard constraints on egress/nat pools or cross-rack bandwidth.

Key proposals (short):
- Admission policy: two-tier admission based on token-rate per-tenant and burst-window. Soft quotas for steady-state; hard admission when 95th percentile QPS + burst > slab capacity.
- Slab elasticity: pre-warmed slabs (warm pool) sized to cover 2x average burst; cold scaling via on-demand slabs with 90s amortized spin-up across OOB scheduler.
- Network slicing: dedicate an egress channel per slab class (latency-sensitive vs batch) with per-slab egress policer to protect shared fabrics.
- Failover choreography: automated fallback to compatible quantized model variant in a different slab class + cross-region drain if local slab exhausted.

Open questions for Thursday:
1) Do you have strict NAT ephemeral port limits per VPC we need to factor into concurrent connection budgeting?
2) Any constraint on east-west cross-rack bandwidth during full-slab warmups?
3) Is a 90s average spin-up acceptable for on-demand slab provisioning, or do you need a 30s SLA for your production tier?

Action items I want to confirm in the meeting:
- EdgeCarve to validate egress port and NAT table headroom (Sanjay)
- Redwood to run a 1-hour soak sim against the capacity model with a fat-tail burst shape and share results (Jonas + Karthik)
- Agree mutual action plan (MAP) with provisioning windows and scale triggers

Thanks — if any of you want to propose a different default policy before the review, reply inline.

—Marissa

Marissa — quick read and a couple of thoughts before the review: great framing. A few technical clarifications from infra sizing side.

1) Admission thresholds: instead of single 95th percentile cut, propose a hysteresis band: admission enforced when rolling 5-min P95 exceeds slab headroom and continues for 2 consecutive 1-min buckets. This avoids flip-flop during transient spikes.

2) Warm-pool strategy: rather than statically reserve 2x avg burst, we can use a sliding warm-pool target that snaps up during sustained increased traffic ( > 10% above baseline for 15m ) — keeps OPEX down.

3) Network slicing: we'll need per-slab egress policers plus an observed RTT budget. If slab A (latency) shares TOR with slab B (batch) we must enforce per-TOR rate limiting otherwise tail latency balloons.

I'll run the 1-hour fat-tail soak in our staging cluster and attach results (throughput/time, avg token latency, queue depth) before the meeting. I can also add a model that simulates NAT ephemeral exhaustion.

--Jonas
Jonas Weber
Sr. Cloud Architect, Redwood Inference

Marissa / team — thanks for the clear runbook. Quick answers from EdgeCarve infra: 

1) NAT ephemeral ports: our current VPC NAT gateway has a soft limit around 65k ephemeral ports but due to other tenants we recommend budgeting ~18k concurrent ephemeral TCP connections per NAT device for long-lived sessions. If you need >18k concurrent upstream connections we need to provision an additional NAT pool or use SNAT chaining.

2) East-west bandwidth: cross-rack 10Gbps per TOR typically; during warmups we see transient spikes up to 7Gbps per rack if many slabs pull weights simultaneously. We can provide a curated warmup window to stagger slab spin-ups by rack.

3) Spin-up SLA: 90s amortized is acceptable for our non-critical lanes. For your latency-critical tier we can aim for 40s via pre-initialized kernels and a standby slab, but that increases reserved GPU time and cost.

We will attach a short NAT headroom report before Thursday. Also: we prefer admission policy to surface an explicit "connection budget" per tenant in addition to token-rate so we can avoid ephemeral exhaustion—happy to sync on the exact metric.

—Sanjay
Sanjay Rao
Head of Infrastructure, EdgeCarve Systems

Thanks — Sanjay, that NAT guidance is exactly the sort of hard constraint we needed. I'm attaching a short synopsis of our soak sim (summary below); full data set will be uploaded to the Drive link.

Soak sim (1hr, fat-tail arrivals) — key takeaways:
- Warm-pool only (no cold-on-demand): sustained 95th token throughput at 78% of nominal slab capacity, median token latency 65ms, P99 token latency 420ms under heady tails.
- With sliding warm-pool + staggered rack warmups (per Jonas' hysteresis) we see P99 drop to ~260ms and throughput hold at 92% capacity with 12% fewer reserved GPUs.
- NAT stress test: ephemeral port exhaustion observed when simulated concurrent upstream connections > 17.5k per NAT; admission controller needs to clamp new long-lived sessions before that point.

Proposed MAP (short):
- Immediate: EdgeCarve validates NAT headroom and confirms warmup staggering windows (Sanjay).
- T+3 days: Redwood to provide final admission policy JSON and slab sizing defaults for review.
- T+7 days: Joint 2-hour runbook rehearsal (warmups + failover) in staging.

I'll drop the full soak CSV to the Drive by EOD.

—Karthik
